name: Illinois

sales.rateNote: State rate of 6.25% on general merchandise (Retailers' Occupation Tax). Qualifying drugs and medical appliances are taxed at a reduced 1% state rate. Since January 1, 2026 the State no longer taxes groceries (see groceries).

local.levies: home rule and non-home rule municipalities and counties, mass transit districts (RTA, Metro-East), park districts, county public safety / public facilities / transportation taxes, county school facility tax; since 2026 also a municipal or county grocery tax of exactly 1%
local.capNote: Local rates change only on January 1 and July 1. The local grocery tax, when adopted by ordinance, must be exactly 1%. No general cap read on an official page.

groceries.note: The State eliminated its 1% tax on groceries on January 1, 2026 (Public Act 103-0781). Municipalities and counties may impose a local grocery tax of exactly 1% by ordinance; more than 600 ordinances had been filed before the change, so most shoppers still pay 1% on groceries. Soft drinks, candy, alcohol and prepared food remain taxed at the general merchandise rate.

clothing.note: Clothing is general merchandise taxed at 6.25% plus local taxes, except during the August 2026 sales tax holiday (state portion cut to 1.25% on items under $125).

prescriptionDrugs.note: Qualifying drugs and medical appliances stay at the reduced 1% state rate after the 2026 grocery reform.

otherRates.note: Tax based on purchase price or fair market value using the RUT-5 chart; flat $25 for motorcycles and ATVs, $15 for some family transfers.

holidays2026.name: Back-to-School State Sales Tax Holiday
holidays2026.items: clothing and footwear priced under $125 per item and certain school supplies (no price limit on supplies); the state portion of the tax drops from 6.25% to 1.25%, local taxes still apply

sales.holidayNote: Created by Public Act 104-0468; it is a reduced-rate holiday (state share cut by 5 points), not a full exemption.

useTax.note: 6.25% on general merchandise and 1% on qualifying drugs and medical appliances bought without Illinois tax. Individuals owing $600 or less ($1,200 married filing jointly) may pay the year's use tax on Form IL-1040; above that, Form ST-44 is due monthly.

facts.text: On January 1, 2026 Illinois became a state with no state tax on groceries, but cities and counties may add a 1% local grocery tax by ordinance, and IDOR received more than 600 such ordinances.
Retailers in a town that adopted the local grocery tax must keep charging 1% on groceries; IDOR issued a compliance alert in 2026 because some stopped collecting it.
New local grocery tax ordinances filed by April 1 take effect July 1; those filed by October 1 take effect the following January 1.
Illinois held a 10-day back-to-school tax holiday from August 7 to 16, 2026, cutting the state share of tax to 1.25% on clothing under $125 and school supplies.
Since January 1, 2025, out-of-state retailers making sales to Illinois customers collect destination-based Retailers' Occupation Tax, including local taxes at the delivery address.
Medicines, including nonprescription items like aspirin and cough medicine, are taxed at a 1% state rate instead of 6.25%.

property.levied: local only: counties, townships, municipalities, school districts and other special districts levy; the Illinois Department of Revenue supervises equalization and exemptions

assessment.text: Outside Cook County, property is assessed at 33 1/3% of fair market value (farmland is assessed on its productivity). Cook County classifies property: residential property is assessed at 10% of market value. A state equalization factor is applied, and property is reassessed every four years (three in Cook County). The Property Tax Extension Limitation Law (PTELL) limits growth of non-home-rule districts' total levies to 5% or CPI, whichever is less, in Cook, the collar counties and counties that adopted it by referendum; it does not cap individual bills.

homestead.name: General Homestead Exemption (Owner-Occupied)
homestead.text: Reduces equalized assessed value (EAV) by the increase above the 1977 EAV, up to $6,000 in most counties, $8,000 in counties contiguous to Cook County and $10,000 in Cook County, for an owner-occupied principal residence.
homestead.applyBy: Chief County Assessment Office (Cook County Assessor in Cook County)

otherRelief.name: Senior Citizens Homestead Exemption
otherRelief.text: Age 65+: EAV reduction of up to $8,000 in Cook and contiguous counties, $5,000 elsewhere.

otherRelief.name: Low-income Senior Citizens Assessment Freeze (SCAFHE)
otherRelief.text: Freezes the EAV of a 65+ owner with household income of $75,000 or less for tax year 2026 ($77,000 for 2027, $79,000 for 2028 and after). File Form PTAX-340 each year.

otherRelief.name: Standard Homestead Exemption for Veterans with Disabilities
otherRelief.text: $2,500 EAV reduction at 30-49% disability, $5,000 at 50-69%, and the first $250,000 of EAV exempt at 70% or more.

otherRelief.name: Homestead Exemption for Persons with Disabilities
Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral
otherRelief.text: Owners 65+ meeting income limits can defer property taxes; the state pays and recovers the amount with interest when the home is sold, up to 80% of the owner's equity.

facts.text: Cook County assesses homes at 10% of market value, while every other Illinois county uses 33 1/3%.
The homestead exemption depends on location: $10,000 of EAV in Cook County, $8,000 in the counties next to Cook, $6,000 elsewhere.
Homeowners may claim an Illinois income tax credit of up to 5% of the property tax paid on their primary residence.
The senior assessment freeze income limit rises by law from $75,000 (tax year 2026) to $77,000 (2027) and $79,000 (2028).
PTELL ('tax caps') covers Cook County since the 1994 levy year and the collar counties (DuPage, Kane, Lake, McHenry, Will) since 1991; 33 other counties adopted it by referendum.
Remodeling is shielded for four years: the Homestead Improvement Exemption covers up to $75,000 of added fair cash value.

uncertain: effectiveSince of the 6.25% state rate not found on an IDOR page; left null.
No statutory cap on local sales tax rates read on an official page (home rule units are not capped by a single figure); cap left null.

The IDOR Use Tax Rates page (research/taxrates/use.html) still mentions 1% on 'qualifying food', while the Use Tax FAQ and Bulletin FY 2026-03 say the state 1% grocery tax ended on January 1, 2026: the newer bulletin was followed.
Property tax due dates are set by each county (Cook County uses two installments); no statewide date published by IDOR, left null.
